title: He Was Guddu for a Decade — Now Ali Fazal Has Prime Video's Biggest Indian Hit in Two Years
excerpt: Raakh, a haunting retelling of the 1978 Ranga-Billa case, has been the #1 non-English series on Prime Video worldwide for two consecutive weeks — and it might be the best Indian OTT show of 2026.
body:
The numbers arrived quietly, the way the show itself does.

Two weeks after its premiere on June 12, **Raakh** — Prime Video's eight-episode crime thriller starring **Ali Fazal**, **Sonali Bendre**, and **Aamir Bashir** — has claimed the #1 non-English series spot on the platform worldwide. Not just in India. *Worldwide.* For two consecutive weeks. It is now officially Prime Video's most-watched new Indian Original in the last two years, and the kind of show that makes you sit in silence for a full minute after the credits roll on the finale.

If you haven't started it yet, clear your evening. All eight episodes are streaming now on Prime Video across 240+ countries — which means whether you're in Houston, Hounslow, or Hyderabad, it's already in your library.

## The Story That Shook a Nation

Raakh is loosely inspired by one of the most horrifying crimes in Indian history: the 1978 Ranga-Billa case, in which two teenage siblings — Geeta and Sanjay Chopra — were kidnapped and murdered in Delhi. The case sent shockwaves through the country and became a defining moment of fear, grief, and reckoning for an entire generation.

The series fictionalises the events — renaming the siblings Suman and Sahil Arora — but preserves the gut-wrenching emotional core. It follows **Sub-Inspector Jayprakash Jatav**, played by Ali Fazal, as he leads a nationwide manhunt to track down two killers hiding in plain sight. The dual-timeline structure — cutting between the investigation and the days leading up to the crime — builds a suffocating tension that never lets up.

Directed by **Prosit Roy** (the filmmaker behind *Pari* and key episodes of *Paatal Lok*) and created by **Anusha Nandakumar** and **Sandeep Saket**, Raakh is not interested in cheap thrills. It is interested in the weight of what violence takes from everyone it touches — the victims, the families, the investigators, and even the perpetrators.

## Ali Fazal Has Never Been Better

Let's be honest: for most of the last decade, Ali Fazal was Guddu Pandit. **Mirzapur** made him a household name — the angry, impulsive gangster with a gun and a grudge. It was a star-making performance, but it also threatened to define him.

Raakh obliterates that box entirely.

As JP, Fazal plays a dismissed rookie cop who is methodical, haunted, and profoundly decent. There is no swagger, no theatrics, no action-hero posturing. Instead, there is restraint — the kind of performance where what the actor doesn't say carries more weight than what he does. Critics have called it his career-best work, and they're right.

> "The response to Raakh has been truly extraordinary. It is incredibly gratifying to see it emerge as Prime Video's #1 non-English series worldwide." — Nikhil Madhok, Head of Originals, Prime Video India

## Sonali Bendre's Devastating Comeback

**Sonali Bendre** as Mona Arora — the mother of the missing children — delivers the kind of performance that reminds you why she was one of the most compelling screen presences of the '90s. Her grief is not loud; it's the kind that sits behind the eyes and never fully leaves. **Aamir Bashir** as the father matches her note for note, and together they create portraits of parental devastation that are almost unbearable to watch.

The supporting cast is equally extraordinary. **Akash Makhija** and **Ramandeep Yadav** as the two killers, Babu and Rajjo, avoid every cliché of the on-screen villain. Makhija is chilling precisely because he's so ordinary; Yadav is heartbreaking because his need to belong is what pulls him into the darkness. **Rakesh Bedi** and **Dibyendu Bhattacharya** round out an ensemble that has no weak link.

## Why the Diaspora Should Care

Raakh's global dominance isn't an accident. The show's themes — justice, morality, how a society processes unthinkable violence — are universal, but its setting is unmistakably Indian. The meticulous recreation of late-1970s Delhi, from the Ambassador cars to the Doordarshan-era interiors, is immersive in a way that will hit particularly hard for anyone who grew up hearing about the Ranga-Billa case from parents or grandparents.

It also arrives at a moment when Indian OTT is producing its most ambitious work. Between **Black Warrant** exploring Tihar from the inside, **Delhi Crime** redefining the procedural, and now Raakh excavating the case that arguably birthed the modern Indian true-crime obsession, Prime Video and Netflix are in an arms race for the soul of Indian crime storytelling.

Raakh isn't just winning that race. It's running in a lane of its own.

## The Verdict

Five stars from Indian.Community. Universal critical acclaim. The #1 non-English series on the planet's second-largest streaming platform. And a finale that has left viewers across social media struggling to articulate what they just experienced.

This is the one. If you watch one Indian show this year, make it **Raakh**.

**Streaming now on Prime Video** in Hindi, with subtitles, across 240+ countries and territories.
